output.headline: Premier League sets out timetable for Manchester City's appeal
output.bodyHtml:
A rules-based process with fixed deadlines is now under way after an independent panel ruled that Manchester City breached the Premier League's financial rules on the vast majority of more than a hundred charges, in a verdict that has shaken English football.

The serial champions now face the possibility of being relegated from the Premier League, or expelled from the competition altogether, after a verdict in the biggest disciplinary case in the history of the sport was finally delivered.

Related: Manchester City timeline: trophies, transfers and more than 100 charges

Neither party was willing to publicly confirm the outcome on Friday, with an appeal process expected to be pursued imminently by City under rules that set firm deadlines for what happens next. Two years after the hearings first began, there is now some clarity as to the scale of City's rule-breaking.

The 134 charges made against City cover the seasons 2009-10 to 2022-23 and cover a number of areas, with the most serious relating to claims that the club failed to provide “accurate financial information” to the league during this time. From season 2009-10 to 2022-23 inclusive City won seven Premier League titles, a Champions League, three FA Cups and six League Cups.

A City spokesperson said: “The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such Manchester City FC's position remains consistent with the club's statement of February 2023.

“The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.”

The Premier League did not comment, citing the confidential nature of the case. Club executives are understood to have learned about the outcome following a shareholders' meeting in central London on Thursday and subsequently signed non-disclosure agreements.

Asked about the news on Friday evening, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, told ITV Granada Reports: “I've only just been made aware of it – I think these are reports at this stage. But if they're confirmed, obviously I will want to look at the report of the independent commission.

“People shouldn't jump to those kind of conclusions. I know, this has been a long process between the club and the Premier League. I think quite a contested process. So I don't think it's as simple as jumping to conclusions. I think we would all need to study the independent commission's report in some considerable detail before reaching any conclusions.”

The verdict was reached more than three and a half years after the 134 charges were first brought and more than two years since disciplinary hearings began. The Premier League rulebook sets a strict timetable for what comes next: any party who wishes to appeal a decision by a judicial panel must do so by email within 14 days of a decision being announced, and under rule W.86 any hearing should conclude no longer than 12 weeks after the first appeal is submitted. Any decision by the appeal board must also be published, alongside full written reasons, within 30 days of the conclusion of the hearing.

Should City fail in their appeal, the judicial panel would then be expected to produce its verdict on the level of sanction applied to the club. Premier League rule W.64 describes the list of punishments available to a panel. Alongside levying a fine, any disciplinary committee could first suspend a club from competition, or levy a points deduction, or in the most extreme circumstances expel a club from competition altogether.

Such is the scale of the charges brought against City that there is no direct comparison to be made with other disciplinary cases. The recent case involving Chelsea, who were found to have breached the FA's rules on agents on 74 occasions, resulted only in a cash fine of £10m but Chelsea were adjudged not to have gained significant sporting advantage from their actions and were praised for self-reporting the misdemeanours, which had occurred under the ownership of Roman Abramovich. Neither of these factors would appear to apply in the City case, given the systemic claims of financial misreporting and the fact that a majority of the charges related to a failure to comply with league rules.

The unprecedented catalogue of charges related to five distinct areas of alleged rule-breaking. More than 80 charges related to a club's obligation to act in “the utmost good faith” when relaying information to the Premier League and to give complete disclosure of any information requested. These claims pointed towards the league's belief that City had given an inaccurate picture of the club's financial situation and withheld documents that might have cast greater light on it.

The rest of the charges related to alleged breaches of profitability and sustainability rules (PSR) and the related Uefa financial fair play regulations. Finally, 20 charges related to the club's obligation to provide “full details of … remuneration”, with breaches being claimed in the rules relating to the payment of players and managers.

The extent of the charge sheet reflected a process that had been a decade in the making. Uefa found City in breach of FFP in 2014, a decision which resulted in City paying a €20m fine. The Football Leaks affair, in which millions of private documents relating to football clubs and players were hacked and made public in 2015, led to reporting on City's affairs and a new investigation from Uefa. By 2020, Uefa had suspended City from the Champions League for “overstating its sponsorship revenue in its accounts”. This suspension was overturned by City on appeal to the court of arbitration for sport.

In December 2018 the Premier League began its own investigation into City. A highly secretive inquiry, which required legal action by the Mail on Sunday to prove it was taking place, it is believed to have been inspired by the Football Leaks revelations and resulted, four years later, in City being charged.
output.standfirst:
• City plan to appeal, and Premier League rules set firm deadlines for what happens next

  • An independent panel has found the club guilty on the vast majority of 134 financial rule-breaking charges, opening the way to sanctions including possible relegation
output.progress: Manchester City say they will appeal, with strict rules requiring any hearing to conclude within 12 weeks and a written decision within 30 days.

output.headline: Burnham rules out snap election to focus on delivering for voters
output.bodyHtml:
Andy Burnham has confirmed he will not call a general election before 2029, ruling out days of speculation that Labour's revival in the polls could tempt him into an early contest.

The prime minister addressed the question repeatedly during a round of broadcast interviews with regional media on Friday, setting out his focus on delivering rather than an early poll.

He said he was “not particularly” tempted by the idea at first, then became firmer, saying he would “knock that dead” and was “not going to do that” because he was focused on getting on with the job.

Asked by ITV Calendar whether the next election would be in 2029, Burnham said: “Well, yes, that's when the next election will be. All of this speculation on an early election – I can knock that dead.

“You know, people want me, new in office, to be getting on with the job of delivering on the things that we've discussed, rather than putting self-serving politics before that, which was what I would be doing if I call an election. I'm not going to do that.”

Talk of an early election had grown during the last week after polls showed Labour pulling into the lead with support in the low 20s, with the Conservatives and Reform neck-and-neck a few points behind.

Westminster sources said Downing Street advisers and MPs had been weighing the merits of an early poll, though even with the right split, Labour would risk losing its majority and having to form a coalition.

The Guardian revealed on Friday that Ravinder Athwal, the economist who wrote Labour's 2024 manifesto, is taking on a senior role advising John Healey, the chancellor, to strengthen his team before the budget — fuelling further speculation that the party's campaign preparations were gathering pace.

Athwal, a Cambridge economics graduate, devised Keir Starmer's five “missions”, which were meant to shape Labour's approach to government.

Healey recruited Athwal as his senior special adviser from the business advisory group Flint Global, previously run by Burnham's chief of staff, James Purnell, a Blair-era cabinet minister.

All parties had stepped up preparations for a potential campaign since Burnham replaced Starmer in the summer, in case he chose to capitalise on the bounce in his popularity.

The prime minister has repeatedly ruled that out, both before and after taking office, telling his regional interviews that his attention was on the party's autumn conference — including setting out more details of a new model for the water industry that increases public control.

He told BBC South: “As we go into the Labour conference, we will set out more thinking about the change that we need to see in the running of water across the country. But it is clear to me that what we've had in the last 30 years is nowhere near good enough and is actually letting the public pay.”

Burnham also confirmed reports that he would not give any exclusive interviews or articles to the Sun, a policy of solidarity with victims of the Hillsborough disaster over the newspaper's coverage of the 1989 tragedy, which falsely blamed Liverpool fans for the deaths of supporters and for which it has since apologised.

Ahead of the conference in Liverpool, Labour members have been cheered by Burnham's takeover, which has led to a modest recovery in the party's popularity.

An MRP poll of more than 8,000 voters, reported by the Guardian this week, showed a significant shift of left-leaning voters towards Burnham's Labour, encouraging those in the party who had been weighing an early election while Reform's ratings ebb and leftwing parties such as the Greens appear to be losing momentum.

Twice as many voters have returned to Labour from the left as from the right since April, according to previously unreleased research, including a seat-by-seat MRP model, conducted by Survation and the progressive activist site 38 Degrees in Burnham's first month as prime minister.

It also showed progressive voters could push Reform UK into fourth place and put Labour within touching distance of a majority if tactical voting were widespread.

Burnham is beginning to attract a significant number of left-leaning voters back to Labour, motivated by a desire to stop Nigel Farage, the results suggest.
output.standfirst: Labour's recovery in the polls had fuelled talk of a snap election, but the prime minister says he will focus on delivering — including reform of the water industry — until 2029
output.progress: Burnham says his autumn conference speech will set out plans to increase public control of the water industry.

output.headline: Ukraine's decentralised network limits scope of Russian internet attacks
output.bodyHtml:
Ukraine's relatively decentralised internet network is helping to blunt the impact of Russia's attacks, even as Moscow opened a new front this week against the country's digital economy, hitting several Kyiv datacentres and internet providers.

The attacks appeared aimed at weakening the digital backbone of the economy. About 100,000 households in Kyiv and the surrounding region suffered temporary internet outages after strikes on Wednesday and Thursday, according to Ukraine's digital transformation ministry.

On Friday, another drone strike in central Kyiv hit the offices of Datagroup, one of Ukraine's largest telecommunications companies, killing four people.

“Russia has targeted major Ukrainian datacentres, seeking to disrupt the flow of information,” Ukraine's foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, wrote on X.

On Thursday, Polish authorities reported a Starlink satellite station in central Poland serving Ukraine had been set on fire, in what appeared to be part of a coordinated attack on Ukraine's internet infrastructure. Local officials described it as an “act of sabotage” linked to Moscow.

Russia has previously targeted Ukraine's datacentres, but attacks on this scale are new.

Related: Russia could attack a Nato country within months, Danish intelligence says

Keeping the country connected has been a priority for the Ukrainian government throughout the war, with authorities looking for ways to ensure mobile and internet providers have enough backup power to keep operating during prolonged electricity outages.

Ukraine's relatively decentralised internet network also makes it harder for individual strikes to cause widespread or prolonged outages across whole cities or regions.

But with winter approaching, officials and industry figures fear repeated Russian attacks could begin to disrupt the networks that keep Ukraine's banks, payment systems and public services running.

“I recommend Kyiv residents gradually prepare for winter … by getting Starlink terminals or other means of maintaining communications,” Serhii Sternenko, a popular blogger and former government adviser, wrote on X.

“The goal of the Russians is not only to strike at the capital's energy infrastructure but also to destroy all datacentres and internet operators,” Sternenko added.

The attacks come amid Russia's intensified strikes on Ukraine's economy, with missiles and new jet-powered drones used against warehouses, petrol stations, ports and other commercial infrastructure, adding further pressure to an economy already strained by nearly five years of full-scale war.

Among the targets on Friday was a warehouse used by the McDonald's fast food restaurant chain outside Kyiv.

Heavy industry has also been hit hard, with Russian strikes disrupting industrial facilities and steel production. This month, Ukraine failed to produce a single tonne of steel for the first time in a century, according to a senior industry official.

Ukraine is struggling to counter a growing wave of new high-speed Russian jet-powered drones, including the Geran-5, while also running critically low on Patriot missiles needed to defend against Russian ballistic and cruise missile attacks.

Speaking to reporters on Friday, the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said Trump had approved granting Ukraine licences to produce Patriot air defence missiles, potentially giving Kyiv a path to manufacture the crucial systems domestically, though experts say it could take years to establish production.

Trump has previously flip-flopped over whether to allow Ukraine to produce Patriots, with the US also facing pressure on its own stocks because of the war in the Middle East.
output.standfirst:
Ukraine's decentralised internet network and efforts to secure backup power are limiting the damage, as Russian attacks on Kyiv's datacentres and internet providers this week killed four people and cut internet to about 100,000 households

  • Ukraine and Russia's long-range drone war
output.progress: Ukrainian authorities are working to give mobile and internet providers enough backup power to keep operating through prolonged electricity outages this winter.

output.headline: Noah Woods remembered as 'happy, cheeky' boy as inquest into his death opens
output.bodyHtml:
Noah Woods, a three-year-old boy his family have asked to be remembered as “the happy little boy that he was”, died after leaving a playground through a gap in a fence and was later found in a nearby pond, an inquest heard.

Noah became separated from a relative after visiting the playground in Merriam Close, Brantham, on the afternoon of 15 September, Suffolk police said.

About 1,300 members of the public joined a search to find Noah, who police said was non-verbal, partially deaf and had been undergoing an assessment for autism.

Met police divers recovered his body from what is known locally as Decoy Pond on the afternoon of 16 September. Suffolk police said his death was not being treated as suspicious.

After the inquest into his death was opened and adjourned in Ipswich on Friday, Noah's family said they would like him to be remembered as “the happy little boy that he was”.

In a statement, they said: “Noah was a happy, cheeky, playful three-year-old boy who loved to laugh, loved to giggle and who brought joy wherever he went. He was part of a loving and caring family, living with his mummy, daddy and his little baby brother. He was at the centre of our world.

“Noah was being assessed for autism, although he had not received a diagnosis. He also had mild hearing loss and was speech delayed.

“Despite the challenges he faced, he was learning every day. He was saying new words all the time and had only just started finding and using his little voice. One of the things we miss most is the special sound of his voice. It was unique, wonderful, and something we will carry with us forever.”

Noah was “the most affectionate” boy who had an “incredibly special” bond with his brother, the statement said.

DCI Matthew Connick told the inquest that on 15 September, Noah, of East Bergholt, Suffolk, was being “looked after by relatives and this was part of a normal routine for Noah”.

He said they walked to an under-fives play area and CCTV footage in the park “showed Noah playing with his relative”. The first piece of footage was timed at 2.13pm and he was last seen playing at 2.37pm, said Connick, who added that the CCTV was motion-activated so did not provide continuous footage.

He said the relative, who was not named at the hearing, had provided a statement to police. The officer said Noah “left through a gap in the fence leading to the memorial garden where he left through an open gate”. He said Noah went in the direction of Decoy Pond and he was “being closely followed by his relative who was trying to keep up with him”.

He said the relative “shouted after him” but after 200 metres Noah could not be seen. “Police were called and a large-scale search operation began,” Connick said.

Noah was found by a Met police diver “approximately 5 metres from the bank and within submerged tree roots”. The depth was estimated at 1.8 metres at that point, he added.

Noah's death was confirmed at 4.31pm by paramedics and his identity was formally confirmed by his mother, Charlie Peck, at Ipswich hospital that evening. A postmortem examination at Addenbrooke's hospital mortuary in Cambridge recorded his medical cause of death as pending further investigation, Connick said.

The Suffolk assistant coroner Jyoti Gill said at the outset of the hearing, which was not attended by the boy's family: “I would like to express my deepest condolences to Noah's family and friends and all those affected by Noah's death.”

She said at the end of the six-minute hearing: “The inquest is adjourned to a date to be fixed in due course.”

Noah's father, Rhys Woods, had paid tribute to his son in a message shared on a community Facebook group last week. He described Noah as the “sweetest and most innocent little boy, with nothing but love to give”, and added: “We are going to miss him so very much.”

Football players paid tribute to Noah during Everton's home match against Ipswich Town on Saturday by wearing black armbands.
output.standfirst: Noah's family have described him as a joyful three-year-old who 'brought joy wherever he went'; an inquest heard he became separated from a relative in Suffolk and was later found dead in a pond

output.headline: Six-year-old's Rubik's Cube world record is a 'dream come true'
output.bodyHtml:
The mother of the six-year-old girl who broke the women's world record for solving a Rubik's Cube in an average time of just over four seconds said the accolade was a “dream come true” for her daughter, who trains for up to three hours a day for competitions.

“She was overjoyed and felt that all her hard work had paid off,” Lin Yangxi told the Guardian of her daughter's feat.

Lian Yunzhi, known as Zhizhi, broke the women's 3x3 average world record at a “speedcubing” event in Guangzhou hosted by the World Cube Association on 16 September. The girl, who is from Chengdu, solved the puzzle in an average time of 4.27 seconds, breaking the record of 4.52 seconds she had set earlier in the month. In some single attempts, she has solved the puzzle in under four seconds.

“The whole school knows her now,” Lin said. “The teacher told me that older students came to her classroom with slips of paper asking for her autograph, crowding the room.

“She has gained a lot of love and attention through cubing.”

Zhizhi's journey from amateur Rubik's Cube hobbyist to world record-holder started at four years old, when her mother took her to speedcubing classes as one of her “seven or eight” extracurricular activities, which include dancing, painting and gymnastics.

Although Zhihi was well-behaved in all her classes, Lin and her husband decided that the speedcubing route “had great potential for her future development, so we proactively chose to invest more time in it.”

Lin said that solving the puzzle helped “improve concentration, memory, logical thinking and spatial awareness”.

“We felt it was really good for her.”

Zhizhi's world-beating success didn't feel inevitable at first. After several months of training, she brought her average time down to eight seconds, but then hit a bottleneck.

“For about three or four months, no matter how she practised, her times didn't improve at all,” Lin said. “To be honest, both as parents and the child, we felt like giving up at that point.”

But after finding a specialist teacher in Shanghai and learning more than 1,300 Rubik's cube formulas, her speeds improved “very quickly”.

Zhizhi now balances training for speedcubing events alongside her kindergarten studies, spending two to three hours on weekdays and up to six hours at the weekend on the puzzle.

Lin said most weekends were spent at speedcubing competitions, which were a chance for Zhizhi to unwind from regular practice and see friends.

Zhizhi used to envy children who had more playtime, her mother said, “but she later told me she no longer envied them, because pursuing her own goals made her truly happy too”.

While physical injuries are rare in speedcubing, Lin monitors Zhihi's eyesight for signs of myopia, a shortsightedness condition that is especially prevalent in China.

Lin said she and her husband felt “extremely nervous” at this month's speedcubing championship, but admired how their daughter “handled the pressure at that crucial moment”.

Zhizhi's mother doesn't see a speedcubing career for her daughter, but said the sport instilled good habits.

“We just wanted to accompany her as far as she could go. It can forge some grit and perseverance in her, which will serve her well in whatever she chooses to pursue in the future.”
output.standfirst: Lin Yangxi says the achievement means everything to her daughter, six-year-old Lian Yunzhi, who now gets autograph requests from fellow pupils after years of dedicated training
output.progress: Zhizhi's parents found a specialist coach in Shanghai and had her learn more than 1,300 formulas after her progress stalled for months.

output.headline: Alan Johnson joins growing push for better-paid UK paternity leave
output.bodyHtml:
Alan Johnson has joined a growing group of MPs and former ministers calling for six weeks of paternity leave paid at 90% of earnings, capped at £1,200 a week and extended to self-employed fathers — a change he says would fix a system in which working-class fathers, entitled only to £187.18 a week for two weeks, are being shortchanged.

Parliament was in recess when Tony Blair called Alan Johnson up to his flat above No 11. The former prime minister was relaxed, padding around in his socks, while his son Leo played with his toys. Johnson, then the education secretary, spoke about his own son from his second marriage, who was a similar age.

“Tony said: ‘Oh you're a father?’” recalled Johnson. “I said: ‘Tony, I had three kids by the age of 20!’ He looked at me and said: ‘So you really are working-class …’”

It may be almost a quarter of a century since Johnson introduced paid paternity leave, as trade and industry secretary — a policy he says needs updating for today's working-class fathers, the former minister has told the Guardian.

He has added his name to a growing number of current and former MPs and senior Labour figures calling for six weeks of paternity leave paid at 90% of earnings, capped at £1,200 a week, with the offer extended to self-employed fathers, who are currently the only parents with no entitlement to paid leave.

The author married his first wife, Judith, when he was 18, adopting her daughter and going on to have two more children by the time he was 20. His fourth child, with his second wife, was born when he was a minister in the New Labour government in his 50s.

Johnson recalls that when his second child was born, he came home from work on a night shift in the postal service to find a note from his wife telling him she had gone to hospital to have a baby. He slept for a few hours and went back to work.

“Men were meant to go down the pub, buy everyone a drink, smoke a cigar, and leave all the kind of hard work to their partners,” he said. “By the time my fourth child was born, it was practically compulsory to be at the birth – things move on and the law has to move with it.”

Working-class fathers are still far less likely to take up the current paternity leave of £187.18 a week for two weeks, among the least generous offerings in Europe. According to analysis of HMRC data by the campaign group the Dad Shift, 90% of paternity leave in 2024-25 was claimed by fathers in the UK's top half of earners – those who generally make more than £37,800 a year – and 95% of claims for shared parental leave were made by fathers or partners in the top 50% bracket.

Many fathers and partners would still be in the position of having to go back to work the day after the birth of a child, just like he did, added Johnson.

“The statistics about who is actually accessing paternity leave is just stunning. It shows that it's a class issue,” he said. “It's great that more prosperous dads are taking paternity leave, but we've got to do something to increase the take-up among the lower paid.”

The Joseph Rowntree Foundation estimates that introducing the new policy of six weeks at 90% of pay in the forthcoming budget would cost the government an additional £1bn, but increased tax receipts from women going back to work could reduce that cost to £220m.

Asked if the government should introduce the change in the next budget, despite the strong economic headwinds faced by the chancellor, John Healey, Johnson was in no doubt. “Absolutely. In government terms, the cost is money down the back of the sofa,” he said. “And actually if the finances are preventing couples from having children, ultimately that is bad for society. Society needs children, mankind needs to procreate. So encouraging childbirth is good for society, full stop.”

The policy would be popular, and unlikely to be opposed, he added. “If it was, in pure political terms, it's a good dividing line for Andy Burnham and the Labour party to take,” he said. “It's an excellent dividing line.”
output.standfirst: Exclusive: The former minister is backing a costed plan for six weeks' paternity leave paid at 90% of earnings before the budget, saying working-class fathers are shortchanged by the current £187.18-a-week, two-week offer
output.progress: Johnson has joined a growing group of MPs backing six weeks' paid leave, which could cost as little as £220m, the Joseph Rowntree Foundation says.

output.headline: Courts side with press in fight for White House access
output.bodyHtml:
A federal judge has already sided with CNN, MS Now and Politico in their fight for White House access, ordering the administration to restore it — but on Saturday the White House blocked CNN from travelling aboard Air Force One, the latest twist in its battle with the news media.

CNN had been scheduled to fly with Donald Trump to Tennessee for a college football game, the network said on Friday. The White House confirmed CNN's exclusion when it did not list the network on guidance sent to the press corps regarding Trump's schedule for Saturday.

CNN's exclusion from Air Force One was first reported by the Washington Post. The White House did not immediately return the Guardian's request for comment.

The incident comes a week after Trump, a vocal critic of what he deems the “fake news media”, revoked White House access for CNN, MS Now and Politico, citing unfavorable reports about his presidency.

“Media Outlets shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES,” Trump wrote then on Truth Social, vowing that similar action would be taken against other outlets.

The extraordinary move prompted swift backlash from the White House press pool, who suspended their video coverage of Trump in protest.

The press pool is a rotating group of journalists charged with covering presidential travel and disseminating written and multimedia reports to news outlets that may not be present at a given White House event. Since the beginning of Trump's second administration in 2025, the White House has decided which outlets cover the president via the pool each day, a task previously coordinated by the White House Correspondents' Association.

In a joint statement Monday, the White House television pool said: “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.”

In a subsequent lawsuit, CNN, MS Now and Politico argued the White House ban was a violation of the first amendment.

The Department of Justice's attorneys countered that the ban was in the interest of national security, pointing to media reports involving “sensitive” and “classified” information.

The US district judge Timothy Kelly sided with the outlets, ordering the Trump administration to restore their White House access.

CNN, MS Now and Politico's journalists sought to enter the White House on Thursday morning, but were not granted entry until midday.

Hours later, CNN's editorial team along with an MS Now reporter were blocked from covering the state dinner commemorating Chinese president Xi Jinping's visit.
output.standfirst: A federal judge has already ordered CNN, MS Now and Politico's White House access restored, but the White House has now blocked CNN from Saturday's Air Force One flight to a Tennessee football game
output.progress: A federal judge already sided with CNN, MS Now and Politico, ordering the administration to restore their White House access after they sued.
